turns.Question: Measure a spectrum once each at the two positions X=37 mm and X=38 mm. Keep Y at 25.25 mm and Z at 0 mm, align the two spectra to the same wavenumber axis, normalize to vector length 1, and compute the cosine similarity.
turns.Ans:
The Raman spectra were measured at X=37 mm and X=38 mm (Y=25.25 mm, Z=0 mm) using a laser power of 40% and an exposure time of 0.2 seconds.

**Analysis Results:**
- **Alignment & Normalization:** The second spectrum was interpolated onto the wavenumber axis of the first to ensure perfect alignment. Both spectra were then normalized to unit vector length (L2 norm).
- **Cosine Similarity:** The computed cosine similarity between the two positions is **0.9998**.

This extremely high value indicates that the chemical composition and structural environment at these two points are nearly identical.

args.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Get the last two measurements
s1 = spectra[-2] # x=37
s2 = spectra[-1] # x=38

x1, y1 = s1['raman_shift'], s1['intensity']
x2, y2 = s2['raman_shift'], s2['intensity']

# Align to a common axis (interpolate y2 onto x1)
y2_interp = np.interp(x1, x2, y2)

# Normalize to vector length 1 (L2 norm)
norm1 = np.linalg.norm(y1)
norm2 = np.linalg.norm(y2_interp)

y1_n = y1 / norm1 if norm1 > 0 else y1
y2_n = y2_interp / norm2 if norm2 > 0 else y2_interp

# Cosine Similarity (Dot product of L2-normalized vectors)
similarity = np.dot(y1_n, y2_n)
print(f"Cosine Similarity between {s1['title']} and {s2['title']}: {similarity:.4f}")

# Plotting
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(x1, y1_n, label=f"Pos 1: {s1['title']}")
plt.plot(x1, y2_n, label=f"Pos 2: {s2['title']}")
plt.title(f"Normalized Spectra Comparison\nCosine Similarity: {similarity:.4f}")
plt.xlabel("Raman Shift (cm-1)")
plt.ylabel("Normalized Intensity")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
